# Bac Exam Skills: Text Analysis, Report Writing and Revision

🎯 **Objectives**
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
- Form and use the passive voice accurately across all the main tenses.
- Choose between active and passive voice for effect, and know when Bac tasks expect each.
- Analyse an unseen text to state its main idea, its tone and the author's purpose.
- Write a formal report with the correct structure, headings and register.
- Plan your revision and manage your time efficiently on exam day.

🔍 **Warm-up**
Compare two sentences about the same fact.
Active: "Tunisian farmers export thousands of tonnes of olive oil every year."
Passive: "Thousands of tonnes of olive oil are exported every year."
Both are correct English, but they do different jobs. The active sentence puts the doer (farmers) in the spotlight; the passive sentence puts the action and the result in the spotlight, because the doer is obvious, unknown or simply less important than the fact itself. This is exactly the choice a good report writer, a good exam candidate and a good reader of texts must be able to make — and it is the thread running through this final revision chapter.

## I. The Passive Voice: Formation and Usage

📘 **Rules and definitions**
The passive voice is formed with the verb "to be" in the required tense, followed by the past participle (V3) of the main verb: be + V3. The tense of the whole sentence is always carried by "be", never by the participle.
- Present simple: Olive oil is exported to Europe.
- Present continuous: New roads are being built in the south.
- Past simple: The bridge was completed in 2019.
- Past continuous: The results were being analysed when the news broke.
- Present perfect: Thousands of jobs have been created this year.
- Past perfect: The report had already been submitted before the meeting.
- Future simple: The new policy will be announced next month.
- Modals: This problem must be solved quickly. / The data can be checked online.
Only transitive verbs (verbs that take a direct object) can be made passive, because that object becomes the new subject. "By + agent" is added only when the doer is important, surprising or specifically asked for; otherwise it is dropped.

📝 **Grammar patterns and usage**
- Active → Passive, step by step: (1) find the object of the active sentence; (2) make it the subject of the passive sentence; (3) put "be" in the same tense as the active verb; (4) add the past participle; (5) keep "by + agent" only if needed.
- Two objects (give, send, offer, show): either object can become the passive subject. "The company sent the workers a warning" → "The workers were sent a warning" (more natural) or "A warning was sent to the workers."
- Passive with modals of obligation and possibility, very common in Bac "Language" sections: should be done, must be respected, can be improved, might be delayed.
- Impersonal passive for reporting general facts or opinions, typical of formal writing: "It is believed that...", "It has been reported that...", "It is said that renewable energy will double by 2030."

🛠️ **Method (transforming a sentence)**
1. Underline the object of the active sentence — this will become the new subject.
2. Identify the tense of the active verb; choose the matching form of "be".
3. Turn the main verb into its past participle.
4. Decide whether the agent is worth keeping; if yes, add "by + agent" at the end.
5. Re-read the passive sentence: does it still make sense and match the original meaning?

✏️ **Worked examples (original)**
1. Active: "The government launched a new employment programme." → Passive: "A new employment programme was launched (by the government)."
2. Active: "Engineers are testing the new bridge this week." → Passive: "The new bridge is being tested (by engineers) this week."
3. Active: "They will publish the exam results on Friday." → Passive: "The exam results will be published on Friday."
4. Active: "You must submit the form before Monday." → Passive: "The form must be submitted before Monday."
5. Active: "Someone has stolen my bicycle." → Passive: "My bicycle has been stolen." (agent dropped: unknown and unimportant)

👀 **Notes**
Use "by" for the doer of the action (by the committee) but "with" for the instrument used (filled with water, covered with dust). The passive is the natural choice in scientific or historical texts, in news headlines, and above all in formal reports — the very register you will practise in section III. Overusing the passive, however, makes writing sound vague and impersonal; a strong Bac answer mixes both voices deliberately.

⚠️ **Common mistakes**
- Forgetting the auxiliary "be": "The letter sent yesterday" instead of "The letter was sent yesterday."
- Using the base form instead of the past participle: "was write" instead of "was written."
- Keeping an unnecessary agent: "The window was broken by someone" instead of simply "The window was broken."
- Trying to make an intransitive verb passive (arrive, happen, occur have no object, so no passive form).
- Changing the tense during the transformation instead of matching the original.

## II. Text Analysis: Main Idea, Tone and Author's Purpose

📘 **Rules and definitions**
Reading comprehension at Bac level is not only about finding facts; it also tests whether you can read *between the lines*. Three notions matter most:
- Main idea: the single central message the whole text is built around — not just its topic, but what the writer wants to say about that topic.
- Tone: the writer's attitude, revealed through word choice (critical, optimistic, alarmed, ironic, nostalgic, neutral...).
- Purpose: why the text was written — to inform, to persuade, to warn, to entertain, to compare, to propose a solution.

📝 **Technique**
- Preview first: read the title and the first and last sentence of each paragraph before reading in full — this usually reveals the structure and the main idea.
- Underline words carrying strong connotation (alarming, promising, unacceptable, remarkable) — these words signal tone.
- Ask "why did the writer choose to write this, and for whom?" to identify purpose; a text that ends with a call to action is usually persuasive, one that simply explains facts is usually informative.
- Distinguish topic (what the text is about, in a few words: "brain drain") from main idea (what it says about that topic, in a full sentence: "brain drain damages developing countries unless governments create better opportunities at home").

🛠️ **Method (four questions)**
1. What is the topic, in one phrase?
2. What is the main idea, in one full sentence, in your own words?
3. What tone-words would you use to describe the writer's attitude, and which expressions in the text prove it?
4. What is the writer's purpose — and how do the structure and the ending support that purpose?

✏️ **Worked example (original short text)**
"Plastic waste now covers vast areas of the ocean, killing marine life at an alarming rate. Yet simple changes — banning single-use bags, recycling more, choosing reusable bottles — could reverse much of the damage within a generation. It is not too late to act, but it soon will be."
- Topic: plastic pollution of the oceans.
- Main idea: plastic pollution is a serious but still reversible problem if we act now.
- Tone: urgent and cautiously hopeful ("alarming rate", "not too late... but it soon will be").
- Purpose: to persuade the reader that action is both necessary and possible.

⚠️ **Common mistakes**
- Confusing the topic with the main idea and answering with a single word or phrase instead of a full sentence.
- Copying a sentence from the text as "the tone" instead of naming an adjective (worried, mocking, hopeful...).
- Ignoring connotation and reading words only for their literal meaning.
- Guessing the purpose from the topic alone rather than from how the text is organised and how it ends.

## III. Formal and Report Writing

📘 **Rules and definitions**
A report is written to inform a reader (often a superior, a committee or the public) about a situation, an investigation or an event, and often to recommend action. Unlike an essay, a report is not narrated in flowing paragraphs of personal opinion: it is organised under clear headings, so that a busy reader can find information quickly. The standard structure is: Title, Introduction (purpose and scope), Findings (organised by heading or numbered point), Recommendations, Conclusion.

📝 **Grammar patterns and register**
- Formal, objective register: no contractions (do not, not don't), no slang, no "I think" — replace with "It appears that...", "The findings suggest that...", "It is recommended that..."
- The passive voice is common in reports, because the focus is on facts and findings, not on who observed them: "It was found that...", "Several problems were identified...", "Improvements are needed in..."
- Headings and numbering replace linking paragraphs: "1. Overcrowding", "2. Lack of resources", rather than "Firstly... Secondly..."
- Recommendations use modal verbs of advice and obligation: should, ought to, need to, it is essential that...

🛠️ **Method (five stages)**
1. Define the purpose of the report and who will read it.
2. List your findings and group them under two or three clear headings.
3. Draft the Introduction last, once you know exactly what the report contains — it should state the purpose in one or two sentences.
4. Write the Findings under headings, in short factual sentences or bullet points.
5. End with Recommendations (concrete, realistic) and a brief Conclusion; proofread for register — no contractions, no personal anecdotes.

✏️ **Worked example (original report extract)**
Title: Report on Library Facilities at [School Name]
Introduction: This report examines the current state of the school library and proposes improvements, following a survey of 120 students.
Findings:
1. Overcrowding — the library has only 30 seats for over 800 students, and is full by 9 a.m. most days.
2. Outdated resources — 60% of students reported that the reference books were more than fifteen years old.
Recommendations: It is recommended that opening hours be extended and that a budget be allocated for new digital resources.
Conclusion: The library plays a central role in student success; the measures above would considerably improve access to it.

⚠️ **Common mistakes**
- Writing the report as a single flowing essay instead of using headings.
- Using contractions or a personal, conversational tone ("I think it's really bad").
- Forgetting the Recommendations section, or giving vague advice ("things should get better").
- Starting with an opinion instead of stating the report's purpose and scope first.

## IV. Final Exam Revision Strategies

📘 **Managing your time on the day**
The Bac English paper typically allows around two hours for Reading Comprehension, Language and Writing. A safe allocation is roughly: 30–35 minutes for reading comprehension (read the text twice, answer in your own words), 25–30 minutes for the language section (grammar, vocabulary, transformations such as passive voice), 40–45 minutes for the writing task (5 minutes planning, 30 minutes writing, 5–10 minutes proofreading), leaving a few minutes at the end to check everything.

🛠️ **Revision method**
1. Build a short revision timetable covering: essay/report writing plans, passive voice and reported speech rules, a personal bank of 15–20 linking words, and the vocabulary lists from each trimester.
2. Practise past papers under real timed conditions, not just reading through notes — timing yourself is the single most effective preparation.
3. Keep an error log: every time you make a grammar mistake in practice, write the rule next to it and revisit that page the following week.
4. Learn flexible paragraph structures (Point–Evidence–Explain, Introduction–Findings–Recommendations) rather than memorising whole essays or reports, since prompts change every year.
5. On revision day minus one, review your error log and your linking-word bank one last time instead of trying to learn new material.

⚠️ **Common mistakes**
- Spending too long on the reading text and rushing the writing task, which usually carries the most marks.
- Skipping the planning stage for the composition or report and writing directly, which leads to disorganised, repetitive answers.
- Ignoring the recommended word count, producing an answer that is far too short or far too long.
- Memorising one fixed essay and forcing it to fit any topic, instead of adapting a flexible structure.
- Leaving no time to proofread for tense, agreement and spelling errors.

⭐ **To remember**
- Passive = be (in the right tense) + past participle; the object of the active sentence becomes the subject; keep "by + agent" only if it adds information.
- To analyse a text: state the topic, then the main idea in a full sentence, then name the tone with adjectives, then explain the purpose.
- A report is organised under headings (Introduction, Findings, Recommendations, Conclusion), written in a formal, impersonal register, often using the passive.
- On exam day: plan your time (reading, language, writing), always plan before you write, and leave time to proofread.
- Flexible structures beat memorised essays — learn the method, not a fixed text.

🔗 **Applications**
These four skills work together far beyond the Bac. The passive voice and a formal register are exactly what is expected in professional emails, official documents, scientific reports and university assignments. The habit of extracting the main idea, tone and purpose of a text is essential for critical reading of news articles, arguments and instructions in any language. And the discipline of timed practice and structured revision is a skill that will serve you in every exam and every deadline you will face after the Bac, at university and at work.

Read the text, then answer the questions.

TEXT
Solar energy is transforming the way Tunisia produces electricity. In the last decade, the cost of solar panels has fallen by more than 80%, making them affordable even for small farms and households. Large solar plants have been built in the south of the country, where sunshine is abundant almost all year round. Supporters argue that solar power could make Tunisia energy-independent within twenty years, reducing its reliance on imported fuel. Yet challenges remain: panels must be maintained regularly, and the electricity grid needs upgrading to handle the new supply efficiently. Still, most experts agree that the country is moving firmly in the right direction.

1) What is the main idea of this text, in one sentence? (2 marks)
2) What tone does the writer use? Justify with one expression from the text. (2 marks)
3) What is the writer's purpose in this text? (2 marks)
4) Find one sentence in the text that uses the passive voice and explain why the passive is used there. (2 marks)

Read the text, then answer the questions.

TEXT
Youth unemployment remains one of Tunisia's most serious challenges. Every year, thousands of graduates leave university with strong qualifications but struggle to find a first job that matches their skills. Many end up accepting positions far below their level, while others choose to emigrate in search of better opportunities abroad. Economists warn that this waste of talent slows down the country's development and discourages young people from investing in further education. Some solutions have been proposed, such as closer cooperation between universities and employers, and support for young entrepreneurs who want to start their own businesses. Without urgent action, however, the problem is likely to grow worse rather than better.

1) What is the main idea of this text? (2 marks)
2) What tone does the writer adopt towards the situation? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
3) What is the writer's purpose: to inform, to entertain, or to warn and propose solutions? Explain. (2 marks)
4) Give a synonym from the text for "get worse". (1 mark)

Write a short formal report (about 120-150 words) on the state of your school canteen, following this structure: Title, Introduction, Findings (at least two headed points), Recommendations, Conclusion. Use a formal, impersonal register and the passive voice where appropriate.

Rewrite the following informal paragraph in a more formal register, suitable for a report. Change contractions, personal opinions and vague vocabulary: "I think the sports hall is really bad. It's too small and it's always full of stuff nobody uses. Someone should fix it soon."

Imagine it is one month before your Bac English exam. Write a short paragraph (80-100 words) describing your personal revision plan for the final month, mentioning: time management, at least one grammar point you will revise (e.g. the passive voice), and one exam-day strategy. Use appropriate linking words.

Rewrite this active paragraph in a more formal, passive register, as it would appear in a report: "We found several problems in the survey. We identified overcrowding as the main issue, and we recommend that the school hire more staff."

Read the text, then answer the questions.

TEXT
For centuries, the Mediterranean has been a bridge between cultures rather than a barrier. Traders, scholars and travellers crossed it constantly, carrying goods, ideas and inventions from one shore to another. Today, migration across this sea is often described only in terms of crisis and danger, and the human stories behind the numbers are easily forgotten. Behind every statistic is a person seeking safety, opportunity or simply a better future for their children. This does not mean that migration raises no real questions - it does - but framing it solely as a threat prevents thoughtful conversations about fair and workable policies. A more balanced narrative, neither naive nor alarmist, is urgently needed.

1) According to the text, how was the Mediterranean traditionally seen? (2 marks)
2) What criticism does the writer make about how migration is discussed today? (2 marks)
3) What is the writer's purpose? Is the text more informative or persuasive? Justify. (2 marks)
4) Identify the tone of the last sentence and explain what it reveals about the writer's stance. (2 marks)

Read the text, then answer the inference question.

TEXT
The new recycling centre opened in March with great fanfare: officials cut a ribbon, journalists took photographs, and the mayor promised it would "transform waste management in the city." Six months later, only one of the three sorting machines is working, and residents report that collection trucks often skip entire streets. The centre's manager says that spare parts have been ordered but have not yet arrived. Meanwhile, the amount of recyclable waste sent to landfill has barely changed since the centre opened.

1) What can you infer about the gap between the opening ceremony and the centre's actual performance? (2 marks)
2) What is the writer's likely attitude towards the officials' promise? Justify using evidence from the text, without quoting a full sentence. (2 marks)

Write a formal report (about 150 words) recommending improvements to public transport in your town, following the structure: Title, Introduction, Findings (two headings), Recommendations, Conclusion. Use the passive voice at least twice and avoid any informal language.

Read the following short text, then answer the questions on main idea, tone, purpose AND transform one sentence into the passive voice - this combines all the skills of this chapter, as in a real Bac exam.

TEXT
Examination stress affects almost every student preparing for the Bac. Long hours of revision, family expectations and the fear of failure combine to create considerable pressure in the months before the exam. Teachers and psychologists increasingly recommend structured revision timetables, regular breaks and enough sleep, arguing that a rested mind performs far better than an exhausted one. Cramming the night before an exam, they warn, does more harm than good. Students who plan their revision calmly, rather than panicking at the last minute, tend to achieve better and more consistent results.

1) State the main idea in one sentence. (2 marks)
2) What is the tone: alarmed, reassuring-and-practical, or mocking? Justify. (2 marks)
3) What is the writer's purpose? (2 marks)
4) Put into the passive: "Teachers and psychologists increasingly recommend structured revision timetables." (2 marks)
